doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: Scat singing, learning Bird solos, and the first lesson with Tristano
summary: She learned scat phrasing from Charlie Parker solos and from Detroit singers Skeeter Speight and LeRoy Mitchell; Mingus took her to Lennie Tristano, who had her learn a Prez solo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Where do you come up with more than shoobie-doobie?

Well I got it from Bird. I mean there was no way in the world that I could try to learn a Bird solo, which was teaching myself this, nobody ever said oh go learn Bird. I was so crazy about bebop music and Bird that I wanted to sing everybody’s solo. Try to sing everybody’s solo. So I learned all these bebop lines. And in so doing there was no room in there for shoobie-doobie. [scats] I mean it’s pretty hard isn’t it?
Yeah. You couldn’t get it out fast enough.
No, no. Not on “Confirmation,” or any of those tunes. So if I’m going to sing “Confirmation,” [scats] I mean I can’t do it. So I just learned in order — and plus I

should also say that I had two wonderful young musicians that were wonderful singers in Detroit, Skeeter Speight and LeRoy Mitchell, we called him Mitch but his real name was LeRoy Mitchell. And those two guys took me under their wing when I was very young. They were young too but they were two young Afro-American musician singers, and I just wanted to do this music so bad. And the only thing was I was young and I drank a lot. And they’d say well we’ll teach you this, but you’ve got to stop drinking. And I did for a while. And they taught me a lot. They had wonderful, wonderful syllables. So I would say, to answer your question again, is that it was really listening to the instrumentalists. When I first went to Lennie Tristano, Mingus took me to Tristano to study. And my first lesson was, “Do this Charlie Parker solo.” And I said, “Well I know it.” And he said, “Oh really?” And I said, “Yeah.” And he said, “Well let’s hear you sing it.” So he put the record on and of course I sang Bird’s solo and everybody else’s solo. Not great, but you know what I mean. I knew it. And he said, “Oh, you do know it.” And I said well you know, then I started feeling like smart ass. You know how you get into it. Well I guess I showed you.

But I knew that I did, you know, but I had low self esteem so that really lifted my self esteem up a couple of notches. He said, “Well I’ll tell you what,” he said, “do you know Prez?” I said, “No.” He said, “All right, so then why don’t you learn a Prez solo?” And so he gave me “Tickle Toe.”
That’s usually the way instructors do too. Instead of — he went backwards on you, right?
Uh huh. That’s right. Yeah. And he waited and he let me go through my whole little ego trip, and then he was so cool. I went wow, I’ll never forget that. I can still see that.
